name: Leases and Fencing Tokens
intent: Give a node temporary ownership of a resource that expires on its own, and use a monotonically increasing token (one that only ever goes up) so the resource itself can refuse a holder whose lease has been lost.
scenario: Worker A holds a 10 second lease to write a shared file. A garbage collection pause freezes it from t=3 to t=18. The lease expires at t=10 and Worker B is granted it. When A wakes up it still believes it is the owner and writes: without fencing tokens the file is corrupted, with them the storage rejects the stale write.
problem: A plain lock held by a crashed node blocks everyone forever, so locks need an expiry. But expiry is a judgement made by one machine's clock about another machine's liveness, and it can be wrong: a holder can be alive yet frozen by a stop-the-world GC, a VM migration, a swapped-out page or a delayed packet. It wakes up after its lease expired and another node was granted it, still believing it is the owner. Checking the lease before acting does not help, because the pause can happen right after the check. Safety cannot depend on the holder noticing.

howItWorks.title: Grant a time-limited lease
howItWorks.text: A node asks the lease service (a replicated store such as etcd, ZooKeeper or Chubby, or a conditional write on an object) for a resource. If nobody holds a live lease it gets one that expires at a deadline. If the holder crashes, the lease simply runs out and the resource becomes available again, which a plain lock cannot do. The grantor measures the duration on its own clock, which is the only clock that matters for expiry.

howItWorks.title: Renew well before expiry
howItWorks.text: A healthy holder renews periodically, typically every one third to one half of the lease duration, so one or two lost renewals do not lose the lease. Kubernetes node heartbeats use a Lease object renewed about every 10 seconds, and leader election defaults are around a 15 second lease with 10 second renew deadline and 2 second retry period. The holder should stop using the lease a safety margin before the grantor will expire it, to absorb clock drift (commonly well under 0.1 percent, so milliseconds per lease) and renewal latency.

howItWorks.title: The hole: pauses and delays make the holder wrong
howItWorks.text: Holder-side checks protect against slow clocks, not against pauses. A holder that checks 'is my lease valid?' and is then frozen for 15 seconds, or whose request sits in a network queue, performs the action after the lease is gone. Stop-the-world pauses of seconds to minutes happen in practice (GC, VM live migration, a laptop lid, a stalled disk), so a lease alone gives mutual exclusion only in the absence of pauses.

howItWorks.title: Issue a fencing token with every grant
howItWorks.text: Each time the lease service grants a lease to a new holder it also returns a number that is strictly larger than any it has issued before: a counter, a Raft log index, a ZooKeeper zxid or znode version, or an etcd revision. The holder must attach that token to every request it sends to the resource.

howItWorks.title: The resource rejects stale tokens
howItWorks.text: The storage remembers the highest token it has accepted and rejects any request with a lower one. A frozen holder wakes up, sends its write with the old token, and is refused; it then learns it lost the lease. Safety now comes from the resource, which sees every write in one order, not from clocks or from the client's good behaviour. This is the same idea as a conditional write (compare-and-swap: write only if the version is unchanged, as with a version number or ETag) and as an epoch number in Raft or Paxos.

howItWorks.title: Tune the duration for failover, not for safety
howItWorks.text: With fencing, the lease duration only decides how fast a crashed holder is replaced and how much renewal traffic you pay for. Short leases (a few seconds) fail over quickly but expire spuriously during GC pauses or network blips and multiply renewal load. Long leases (30 to 60 seconds or more) are calm but leave the resource unowned for that long after a real crash.

pros: A crashed or partitioned holder cannot block the resource forever, which a plain lock cannot guarantee
Fencing tokens make correctness independent of clocks, GC pauses and network delays
The check is one integer comparison in the resource, so it is cheap and easy to reason about
The lease duration becomes a pure tuning knob for failover time versus renewal load
cons: Without fencing, a lease gives only best-effort mutual exclusion: two owners are possible
The resource must cooperate and persist the highest token, and many third-party systems cannot
After a crash the resource stays unavailable for up to the full lease duration
Renewals are traffic and a dependency on the lease service, and a lease service outage expires every lease at once
Holders must handle losing the lease at any instruction and stop work safely
whenToUse: Exactly one writer or leader must act on a shared resource and holders can crash or stall
Leader leases for lease-based reads (Raft leader leases, Spanner leader leases) where the leader serves reads locally while its lease is valid
Coordinating batch workers, schedulers or singleton jobs where a duplicate run corrupts data
Failure detection with cheap soft state, such as node heartbeats or session leases
whenNotToUse: Efficiency-only locking, where a rare duplicate run just wastes some work: a plain best-effort lease is enough
Operations that are already idempotent or protected by a conditional write on the data itself, which makes the lock redundant
When the resource cannot check a token and you cannot change it: a lease then gives a false sense of safety and you need a different design
As a replacement for consensus: the lease service itself must be a replicated, linearizable store (it behaves like one up-to-date copy)
pitfalls: Checking lease validity on the client right before the write and calling that safe: the pause happens after the check
Taking the token from the lease service and checking it in the client or a proxy, instead of in the storage that applies the write
Tokens that are not strictly increasing across failovers, for example a counter held in memory that restarts from zero
Using wall-clock time for the expiry decision: NTP steps or leap-second handling can move it backwards, so use a monotonic clock (one that never goes backwards) on each side
Choosing a lease shorter than your worst pause, so leases expire constantly and the owner keeps changing (flapping)
Forgetting that the old holder may have started a side effect (an email, an external API call) that no token can undo

roles.label: Lease service
roles.description: Grants leases with an expiry and a strictly increasing fencing token, using its own clock.

roles.label: Worker
roles.description: Acquires, renews and uses a lease, and attaches its token to every request. May pause without knowing.

roles.label: Storage
roles.description: The protected resource. Remembers the highest token seen and rejects anything lower.

quiz.question: Worker A holds a 10 second lease on a shared file and is frozen by a 15 second garbage collection pause. The lease expires and worker B is granted it. When A wakes, it writes to the file. Which design prevents the corruption?
options: Each grant carries an increasing fencing token, and the storage rejects lower tokens
Worker A checks that its lease is still valid immediately before it performs each write
The lease is lengthened to 60 seconds, which is longer than the pause that was observed
Worker A renews the lease every second instead of every few seconds
quiz.explanation: The pause can happen right after any client-side check, so only the resource can safely reject a stale holder. A longer lease or faster renewal narrows the window but cannot cover a pause that outlasts it.

quiz.question: A lease service issues fencing tokens from an in-memory counter. It crashes and restarts from 0. The storage has already accepted token 57 from the previous holder. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing, since each new grant is a separate event and the storage only compares equal tokens
Low tokens are rejected as stale, so tokens must come from a replicated increasing source
The storage accepts any token it has not seen before, so both holders can write at once; use a random UUID instead
The storage simply resets its record, so tokens work again; the only cost is one rejected write
quiz.explanation: Fencing relies on tokens that never go backwards across failovers. A counter that restarts breaks the ordering, and a random UUID cannot be compared. Use something like an etcd revision or a Raft log index.

quiz.question: A system uses leases with correct fencing, checked in the storage. The lease is 5 seconds, and pauses of up to 8 seconds make leases expire and the owner change often, though data stays correct. You can accept up to 30 seconds of failover. What is the best action?
options: Shorten the lease to 1 second so ownership is decided before any pause can matter at all, even a long one
Drop fencing, since the constant flapping shows that the tokens themselves are the real cause of it
Lengthen the lease to about 30 seconds, since it only trades failover speed for flapping
Keep 5 seconds and stop renewing, so that a pause never extends a lease
quiz.explanation: With fencing in place, safety no longer depends on the duration, so the choice is only failover speed versus spurious expiry. A shorter lease would flap even more, and removing the tokens would give up the safety that is working. Not renewing makes expiry sooner, so it flaps more.
